claim: The mouse Suv39h2 enzyme differs from Suv39h1 by containing an N-terminal basic domain that facilitates retention at mitotic chromatin.
source: We show here that the mouse Suv39h2 enzyme differs from Suv39h1 by containing an N-terminal basic domain that facilitates retention at mitotic chromatin and provides an additional affinity for major satellite repeat RNA.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing differential chromatin retention of Suv39h2 versus Suv39h1 at mitotic chromatin (Figure 2H, 2J) and by deletion mutant analysis (Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP).

claim: The N-terminal basic domain of Suv39h2 provides an additional affinity for major satellite repeat RNA.
source: We show here that the mouse Suv39h2 enzyme differs from Suv39h1 by containing an N-terminal basic domain that facilitates retention at mitotic chromatin and provides an additional affinity for major satellite repeat RNA.
evidence: Supported by in vitro RNA binding assays showing that the basic domain of Suv39h2 binds to MSR RNA (Figure 3B, 3C, 3D).

claim: Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 exclusively associate with poly-nucleosomes.
source: To analyze an RNA-dependent interaction with chromatin, we purified native nucleosomes from mouse ES cells and detect that Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 exclusively associate with poly-nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation experiments showing Suv39h enzymes in poly-nucleosomal fractions (Figure 5A).

claim: The association of Suv39h enzymes with poly-nucleosomes is attenuated upon RNaseH incubation.
source: This association was attenuated upon RNaseH incubation and entirely lost upon RNaseA digestion of native chromatin.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation showing altered sedimentation profiles after RNaseH treatment (Figure 5A, second panel).

claim: The association of Suv39h enzymes with poly-nucleosomes is entirely lost upon RNaseA digestion of native chromatin.
source: This association was attenuated upon RNaseH incubation and entirely lost upon RNaseA digestion of native chromatin.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation showing loss of Suv39h enzymes from nucleosomal fractions after RNaseA treatment (Figure 5A, third and fourth panels).

claim: Major satellite repeat transcripts remain chromatin-associated.
source: Major satellite repeat transcripts remain chromatin-associated and have a secondary structure that favors RNA:DNA hybrid formation.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR detection of MSR RNA in nucleosomal fractions (Figure 5B), subcellular fractionation showing ~80% of MSR RNA in chromatin (Figure 5—figure supplement 3), and RNA-seq data (Figure 5C).

claim: Major satellite repeat transcripts have a secondary structure that favors RNA:DNA hybrid formation.
source: Major satellite repeat transcripts remain chromatin-associated and have a secondary structure that favors RNA:DNA hybrid formation.
evidence: Supported by SHAPE analysis showing extended single-stranded regions in MSR RNA (Figure 4B), RNaseH sensitivity of MSR RNA (Figure 6A, 6B), and RDIP experiments with S9.6 antibody (Figure 6C).

claim: The full-length mouse Suv39h2 protein is 477 amino acids.
source: Suv39h2 differs from Suv39h1 by containing an N-terminal basic domain (amino acid position 1–81) giving rise to a predicted gene product of 477 amino acids (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by molecular cloning and sequencing of full-length Suv39h2 cDNA and Western blot detection of endogenous Suv39h2 at 53 kDa (Figure 1B).

claim: The N-terminal basic domain of Suv39h2 spans amino acids 1-81.
source: Suv39h2 differs from Suv39h1 by containing an N-terminal basic domain (amino acid position 1–81) giving rise to a predicted gene product of 477 amino acids (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis and domain structure representation (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Endogenous Suv39h1 is detected at 48 kDa.
source: Immunoblotting with a Suv39h1 antibody indicated endogenous Suv39h1 (48 kDa) in wild type but not in Suv39h double-null (Suv39h dn) cells (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of chromatin extracts (Figure 1B).

claim: Endogenous Suv39h2 is detected at 53 kDa.
source: By contrast, a Suv39h2 antibody recognizes an endogenous protein of 53 kDa in both ES cells and iMEF, which is not detected in the Suv39h dn cells.
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis with multiple Suv39h2 antibodies (Figure 1B).

claim: Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 can independently re-establish H3K9me3 in Suv39h double-null mouse ES cells.
source: All Suv39h-EGFP products can re-establish H3K9me3 to wild-type levels (Figure 1D) and independently localize to heterochromatic foci (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis showing H3K9me3 levels in rescued cell lines (Figure 1D) and ChIP analysis (Figure 2C, 2G).

claim: Suv39h1-EGFP, Suv39h2-EGFP, and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP independently localize to heterochromatic foci in interphase.
source: All Suv39h-EGFP products can re-establish H3K9me3 to wild-type levels (Figure 1D) and independently localize to heterochromatic foci (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence analysis showing colocalization with DAPI-positive heterochromatic foci (Figure 2A).

claim: Suv39h2-EGFP and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP can fully restore MSR silencing in Suv39h double-null ES cells.
source: While Suv39h2-EGFP and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP can fully restore MSR silencing, Suv39h1-EGFP still allows two-fold higher MSR transcript levels as compared to wild type ES cells (Figure 2B), although the H3K9me3 ChIP signal is similar for all three Suv39h-EGFP cell lines (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of MSR transcripts in rescued cell lines (Figure 2B).

claim: Suv39h1-EGFP allows two-fold higher MSR transcript levels compared to wild type ES cells.
source: While Suv39h2-EGFP and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP can fully restore MSR silencing, Suv39h1-EGFP still allows two-fold higher MSR transcript levels as compared to wild type ES cells (Figure 2B), although the H3K9me3 ChIP signal is similar for all three Suv39h-EGFP cell lines (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of MSR transcripts (Figure 2B).

claim: The H3K9me3 ChIP signal at MSR is similar for Suv39h1-EGFP, Suv39h2-EGFP, and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP cell lines.
source: While Suv39h2-EGFP and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP can fully restore MSR silencing, Suv39h1-EGFP still allows two-fold higher MSR transcript levels as compared to wild type ES cells (Figure 2B), although the H3K9me3 ChIP signal is similar for all three Suv39h-EGFP cell lines (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR analysis at major satellite repeats (Figure 2C).

claim: Suv39h1-EGFP is largely absent from mitotic chromosomes.
source: At condensing chromosomes and during pro-metaphase, full-length Suv39h1-EGFP exhibits a broad and diffuse chromosomal pattern (data not shown), but then is largely absent from mitotic chromosomes, although pericentric H3K9me3 persists (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by confocal immunofluorescence analysis of nocodazole-synchronized cells (Figure 2D, 2E).

claim: Pericentric H3K9me3 persists on mitotic chromosomes even when Suv39h1-EGFP is absent.
source: At condensing chromosomes and during pro-metaphase, full-length Suv39h1-EGFP exhibits a broad and diffuse chromosomal pattern (data not shown), but then is largely absent from mitotic chromosomes, although pericentric H3K9me3 persists (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence showing H3K9me3 signal at pericentric regions in the absence of Suv39h1-EGFP (Figure 2D).

claim: Suv39h2-EGFP displays focal accumulation at pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes.
source: In striking contrast, Suv39h2-EGFP displays focal accumulation with the pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes that is accompanied by higher levels of H3K9me3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by confocal immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 2D, 2E).

claim: Suv39h2-EGFP accumulation at pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes is accompanied by higher levels of H3K9me3.
source: In striking contrast, Suv39h2-EGFP displays focal accumulation with the pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes that is accompanied by higher levels of H3K9me3 (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence showing colocalization of Suv39h2-EGFP and H3K9me3 signals (Figure 2D).

claim: The Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant has partially lost focal accumulation at pericentric heterochromatin of mitotic chromosomes.
source: While the Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant is still enriched at some, but not all, pericentric regions of mitotic chromosomes, it also displays a broader distribution along the chromosomal arms. Larger images of this high resolution microscopy confirm that the Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant has partially lost the focal accumulation at pericentric heterochromatin of mitotic chromosomes (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by confocal immunofluorescence analysis (Figure 2D, 2E).

claim: MSR transcripts are derepressed in Suv39h double-null ES cells.
source: There is significant derepression of MSR in Suv39h dn mouse ES cells (Martens et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR data (Figure 2B, 2F) and cited reference (Martens et al., 2005).

claim: In nocodazole-synchronized Suv39h double-null ES cells, MSR transcripts are similarly derepressed as in interphase cells.
source: In nocodazole-synchronized Suv39h dn ES cells, MSR transcripts are similarly derepressed as compared to interphase cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis comparing unsynchronized and nocodazole-synchronized cells (Figure 2B, 2F).

claim: Full-length Suv39h1-EGFP and full-length Suv39h2-EGFP silence MSR expression to levels lower than wild type ES cells in nocodazole-synchronized cells.
source: While both full-length Suv39h1-EGFP and full-length Suv39h2-EGFP products silence MSR expression to levels even lower than those observed in wild type ES cells, the Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant could only repress transcription to levels near to wild type ES cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of nocodazole-synchronized cells (Figure 2F).

claim: The Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant represses MSR transcription to levels near wild type ES cells in nocodazole-synchronized cells.
source: While both full-length Suv39h1-EGFP and full-length Suv39h2-EGFP products silence MSR expression to levels even lower than those observed in wild type ES cells, the Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant could only repress transcription to levels near to wild type ES cells (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis (Figure 2F).

claim: The H3K9me3 ChIP signal at MSR is modestly reduced in Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP ES cells in nocodazole-synchronized conditions.
source: The H3K9me3 ChIP signal at the MSR was also modestly reduced in the Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP ES cells (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by ChIP-qPCR analysis of nocodazole-synchronized cells (Figure 2G).

claim: Endogenous Suv39h1 and Suv39h1-EGFP show rapid solubilization during MNase digestion in nocodazole-arrested cells.
source: In pronounced difference to interphase, endogenous Suv39h1 and Suv39h1-EGFP showed rapid solubilization already during the first 4 min of MNase digestion (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by chromatin release assay with progressive MNase digestion (Figure 2H).

claim: Endogenous Suv39h2 and Suv39h2-EGFP largely remain chromatin associated after 10 min of MNase digestion in nocodazole-arrested cells.
source: By contrast, endogenous Suv39h2 and Suv39h2-EGFP largely remained chromatin associated, even after 10 min of MNase digestion.
evidence: Supported by chromatin release assay (Figure 2J).

claim: The Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant is rapidly released into the soluble fraction during MNase digestion in nocodazole-arrested cells.
source: Noticeably, the Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP mutant was rapidly released into the soluble fraction, with more than 50% of the protein being recovered in the supernatant after 4–6 min of MNase digestion (Figure 2J).
evidence: Supported by chromatin release assay (Figure 2J).

claim: The basic domain of Suv39h2 plays a role in stabilizing the association of Suv39h2 with mitotic chromatin.
source: These results show that Suv39h2 and, to a much lesser degree Suv39h1, robustly interacts with mitotic chromatin and resists solubilization by MNase digestion. In addition, the data also indicate a role for the basic domain of Suv39h2 in stabilizing the association of the Suv39h2 enzyme with mitotic chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of Suv39h2-EGFP and Suv39h2-D(T3K81)-EGFP chromatin release profiles (Figure 2J).

claim: The basic domain of Suv39h2 harbors 22 basic residues, of which 19 are arginines.
source: The basic domain of Suv39h2 harbors 22 basic residues, of which 19 are arginines (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: The basic domain of Suv39h2 shows modest similarity with RNA binding factors involved in RNA splicing and RNA processing.
source: Amino acid alignment of this basic domain (aa 1–81) with arginine-rich proteins that were filtered from the SwissProt database reveals modest similarity with RNA binding factors involved in RNA splicing and RNA processing (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment analysis (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).

claim: The basic domain of Suv39h2 most closely resembles the arginine-rich motif (ARM) RNA binding domain.
source: In this respect, the basic domain of Suv39h2 most closely resembles one common RNA binding domain, the arginine-rich motif (ARM) (Bayer et al., 2005; Casu et al., 2013).
evidence: Based on sequence analysis and comparison with known RNA binding domains, supported by cited references (Bayer et al., 2005; Casu et al., 2013).

claim: Full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2 displays robust band-shift of MSR-F RNA with KD = 0.8 μM.
source: Under these conditions and over a protein range from 16 nM to 2 μM, we observed robust band-shift of MSR-F RNA (KD = 0.8 μM) and of MSR-R RNA (KD = 0.4 μM) with full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2 (Figure 3B, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by EMSA with in vitro transcribed MSR RNA (Figure 3B).

claim: Full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2 displays robust band-shift of MSR-R RNA with KD = 0.4 μM.
source: Under these conditions and over a protein range from 16 nM to 2 μM, we observed robust band-shift of MSR-F RNA (KD = 0.8 μM) and of MSR-R RNA (KD = 0.4 μM) with full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2 (Figure 3B, upper panel).
evidence: Supported by EMSA (Figure 3B).

claim: Full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h1 displays 3-8 fold weaker RNA binding affinity compared to full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2.
source: By contrast, full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h1 displayed 3–8 fold weaker binding affinity.
evidence: Supported by comparison of EMSA results for Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 (Figure 3B).

claim: Deletion of the extended basic domain (aa 1-116) significantly reduces RNA binding capacity of Suv39h2 to levels comparable with Suv39h1.
source: Deletion of an extended basic domain (aa 1–116) significantly reduced RNA binding capacity of Suv39h2 (6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2ΔBD) to levels comparable with 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h1, whereas a construct that only expresses this extended basic domain (aa 1–117) of Suv39h2 (6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2basicD(1-117)) maintained high-affinity (KD = 0.4–0.6 μM) RNA interaction (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by EMSA with deletion mutants (Figure 3B).

claim: The extended basic domain (aa 1-117) of Suv39h2 maintains high-affinity RNA interaction with KD = 0.4-0.6 μM.
source: Deletion of an extended basic domain (aa 1–116) significantly reduced RNA binding capacity of Suv39h2 (6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2ΔBD) to levels comparable with 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h1, whereas a construct that only expresses this extended basic domain (aa 1–117) of Suv39h2 (6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2basicD(1-117)) maintained high-affinity (KD = 0.4–0.6 μM) RNA interaction (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: Supported by EMSA (Figure 3B).

claim: Full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 do not show robust binding to LINE L1MdA 5'UTR transcripts.
source: As a control, we also probed the full-length 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 and the 6xHis-MBP-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) product for binding to 3'-Cy5-labeled forward or reverse IVT LINE L1MdA 5'UTR transcripts (208 nt) and did not observe robust RNA interaction (Figure 3B, lower panels).
evidence: Supported by EMSA with LINE L1MdA 5'UTR RNA (Figure 3B, lower panels).

claim: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) does not bind to ssDNA and dsDNA.
source: The data show (Figure 3C) that the extended basic domain of Suv39h2 does not bind to ssDNA and dsDNA and there is also no interaction with dsRNA or DNA:RNA hybrids.
evidence: Supported by EMSA with various nucleic acid substrates (Figure 3C).

claim: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) does not interact with dsRNA or DNA:RNA hybrids.
source: The data show (Figure 3C) that the extended basic domain of Suv39h2 does not bind to ssDNA and dsDNA and there is also no interaction with dsRNA or DNA:RNA hybrids.
evidence: Supported by EMSA (Figure 3C).

claim: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) robustly binds to ssMSR-F and ssMSR-R RNA oligonucleotides.
source: Instead, GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) robustly binds to ssMSR-F and ssMSR-R RNA oligonucleotides.
evidence: Supported by EMSA (Figure 3C).

claim: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) displays highest affinity for MSR and TERRA RNA (KD ≤ 2 μM).
source: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) displayed highest affinity for MSR and TERRA RNA (KD ≤ 2 μM), intermediate binding to pRNA, Oct4P4 RNA, minor satellite repeat RNA and LINE L1MdA 5'UTR forward RNA (KD > 2 μM) but did not interact with LINE L1MdA 5'UTR reverse RNA, SINE B1 repeat RNA or with an unstructured poly(A) RNA control (Figure 3D, Figure 4A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by EMSA with multiple RNA oligonucleotides (Figure 3D, Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) shows intermediate binding to pRNA, Oct4P4 RNA, minor satellite repeat RNA and LINE L1MdA 5'UTR forward RNA (KD > 2 μM).
source: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) displayed highest affinity for MSR and TERRA RNA (KD ≤ 2 μM), intermediate binding to pRNA, Oct4P4 RNA, minor satellite repeat RNA and LINE L1MdA 5'UTR forward RNA (KD > 2 μM) but did not interact with LINE L1MdA 5'UTR reverse RNA, SINE B1 repeat RNA or with an unstructured poly(A) RNA control (Figure 3D, Figure 4A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by EMSA (Figure 3D, Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) does not interact with LINE L1MdA 5'UTR reverse RNA, SINE B1 repeat RNA or poly(A) RNA.
source: GST-Suv39h2basicD(1-117) displayed highest affinity for MSR and TERRA RNA (KD ≤ 2 μM), intermediate binding to pRNA, Oct4P4 RNA, minor satellite repeat RNA and LINE L1MdA 5'UTR forward RNA (KD > 2 μM) but did not interact with LINE L1MdA 5'UTR reverse RNA, SINE B1 repeat RNA or with an unstructured poly(A) RNA control (Figure 3D, Figure 4A and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by EMSA (Figure 3D, Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: GST-HP1α does not show robust binding to Oct4P4, MSR or SINE B1 RNA within a 125 nM to 2 μM ligand concentration range.
source: For comparison, we used GST-HP1α and could not detect robust binding to Oct4P4, MSR or SINE B1 RNA within a 125 nM to 2 μM ligand concentration range (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by EMSA with GST-HP1α (Figure 3D).

claim: MSR transcript sequences are A/U-rich (64%).
source: MSR transcript sequences are A/U-rich (64%), whereas the 5'UTR of LINE L1MdA is G/C-rich (61%).
evidence: Based on sequence composition analysis.

claim: The 5'UTR of LINE L1MdA is G/C-rich (61%).
source: MSR transcript sequences are A/U-rich (64%), whereas the 5'UTR of LINE L1MdA is G/C-rich (61%).
evidence: Based on sequence composition analysis.

claim: SHAPE-directed RNA structural modeling shows that A/U-rich MSR RNA has extended sections of ssRNA.
source: This SHAPE-directed RNA structural modeling shows that the A/U-rich MSR RNA (for both forward and reverse strands) has extended sections of ssRNA, whereas the LINE L1MdA 5'UTR RNA are primarily folded into dsRNA (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by SHAPE analysis and RNA structural modeling (Figure 4B).

claim: LINE L1MdA 5'UTR RNA are primarily folded into dsRNA.
source: This SHAPE-directed RNA structural modeling shows that the A/U-rich MSR RNA (for both forward and reverse strands) has extended sections of ssRNA, whereas the LINE L1MdA 5'UTR RNA are primarily folded into dsRNA (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: Supported by SHAPE analysis and RNA structural modeling (Figure 4C).

claim: RNA sequences with the highest degree of predicted single-stranded regions (MSR and TERRA) are favored substrates for binding by the extended basic domain of Suv39h2.
source: In silico structural modeling (Materials and methods) of the 12 distinct RNA oligonucleotides reveals that RNA sequences with the highest degree of predicted single-stranded regions (MSR and TERRA) appear as favored substrates for binding by the extended basic domain of Suv39h2, whereas RNA sequences with the lowest degree of predicted single-stranded regions (L1MdA 5'UTR-R and SINE B1) are not bound (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by in silico structural prediction and correlation with EMSA binding data (Figure 4D).

claim: RNA sequences with the lowest degree of predicted single-stranded regions (L1MdA 5'UTR-R and SINE B1) are not bound by the extended basic domain of Suv39h2.
source: In silico structural modeling (Materials and methods) of the 12 distinct RNA oligonucleotides reveals that RNA sequences with the highest degree of predicted single-stranded regions (MSR and TERRA) appear as favored substrates for binding by the extended basic domain of Suv39h2, whereas RNA sequences with the lowest degree of predicted single-stranded regions (L1MdA 5'UTR-R and SINE B1) are not bound (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by in silico structural prediction and EMSA data (Figure 4D).

claim: All three Suv39h-EGFP products are primarily enriched in poly-nucleosomal fractions in RNase-untreated samples.
source: In RNase-untreated samples, all three Suv39h-EGFP products are primarily enriched in poly-nucleosomal fractions and not in the nucleosome-free fractions (Figure 5A, first panel).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation and Western blot analysis (Figure 5A, first panel).

claim: Suv39h2-EGFP and Suv39h2(T3K81)-EGFP display preference for association with higher-order nucleosomes (fractions 12-17).
source: Suv39h2-EGFP and the Suv39h2(T3K81)-EGFP mutant display preference for association with higher-order nucleosomes (fractions 12–17), whereas Suv39h1-EGFP shows a broader fractionation profile that extends into mono-nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation (Figure 5A, first panel).

claim: Suv39h1-EGFP shows a broader fractionation profile that extends into mono-nucleosomes.
source: Suv39h2-EGFP and the Suv39h2(T3K81)-EGFP mutant display preference for association with higher-order nucleosomes (fractions 12–17), whereas Suv39h1-EGFP shows a broader fractionation profile that extends into mono-nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation (Figure 5A, first panel).

claim: Dnmt3a accumulates with nucleosomes (fractions 11-15) but much less with higher-order poly-nucleosomes.
source: In agreement with previous findings (Jeong et al., 2009), Dnmt3a also accumulates with nucleosomes (fractions 11–15), but much less with the higher-order poly-nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation (Figure 5A, first panel) and cited reference (Jeong et al., 2009).

claim: HP1α sediments in the nucleosome-free fractions and is only marginally distributed with nucleosomes.
source: By contrast, HP1α sedimented in the nucleosome-free fractions and was only marginally distributed with nucleosomes.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation (Figure 5A, first panel).

claim: RNaseH treatment results in buildup of Suv39h-EGFP constructs and H3K9me3, but not Dnmt3a and HP1α, in the pellet.
source: In addition, RNaseH treatment resulted in the buildup of the three Suv39h-EGFP constructs and of H3K9me3, but not of Dnmt3a and HP1α, in the pellet (Figure 5A, second panel).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation after RNaseH treatment (Figure 5A, second panel).

claim: RNaseA (350 mM salt) digestion results in partial dissolution of the nucleosomal ladder and loss of higher-order nucleosomes in fractions 14-17.
source: RNaseA (350 mM salt) digestion of MNase solubilized chromatin resulted in partial dissolution of the nucleosomal ladder and the loss of higher-order nucleosomes in fractions 14–17 (Figure 5A, third panel).
evidence: Supported by DNA gel analysis of sucrose gradient fractions (Figure 5A, third panel).

claim: RNaseA (350 mM salt) digestion shifts full-length Suv39h1-EGFP and Suv39h2-EGFP towards mono- and di-nucleosomes and into the highest molecular weight fraction of nucleosome-free material.
source: While the sedimentation of Dnmt3a and HP1α remained largely unaltered, both full-length Suv39h1-EGFP and full-length Suv39h2-EGFP were significantly shifted towards mono- and di-nucleosomes and into the highest molecular weight fraction of the nucleosome-free material.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation after RNaseA (350 mM salt) treatment (Figure 5A, third panel).

claim: RNaseA (350 mM salt) digestion specifically abrogates chromatin association of the Suv39h2(T3K81)-EGFP mutant.
source: Remarkably, RNaseA (350 mM salt) digestion specifically abrogated chromatin association of the Suv39h2(T3K81)-EGFP mutant, which could no longer be detected in the nucleosomal or nucleosome-free fractions (Figure 5A, third panel).
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation showing loss of Suv39h2(T3K81)-EGFP signal (Figure 5A, third panel).

claim: RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion results in nearly full collapse of the nucleosomal ladder where all but mono- or residual di-nucleosomes can be recovered.
source: This low salt condition enhances the activity of RNaseA (Figure 5—figure supplement 1) and resulted in a nearly full collapse of the nucleosomal ladder where all but mono- or residual di-nucleosomes can be recovered (Figure 5A, fourth panel).
evidence: Supported by DNA gel analysis after RNaseA (100 mM salt) treatment (Figure 5A, fourth panel).

claim: None of the Suv39h-EGFP products can be detected in nucleosomal or chromatin-free fractions after RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion, and all accumulate in the pellet.
source: Further, none of the Suv39h-EGFP products could be detected in the nucleosomal or the chromatin-free fractions and all accumulate in the pellet.
evidence: Supported by sucrose gradient fractionation after RNaseA (100 mM salt) treatment (Figure 5A, fourth panel).

claim: Dnmt3a is still detected in fractions containing residual amounts of di- to tri-nucleosomes after RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion.
source: Importantly, not all nucleosome association was lost upon RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion, since Dnmt3a was still detected in the fractions containing residual amounts of di- to tri-nucleosomes and H3K9me3 (Figure 5A, fourth panel).
evidence: Supported by Western blot analysis of sucrose gradient fractions (Figure 5A, fourth panel).

claim: MSR RNA shows progressive enrichment in nucleosome fractions but not in nucleosome-free fractions.
source: This analysis identified progressive enrichment of MSR RNA in the nucleosome fractions but not in the nucleosome-free fractions and also revealed higher MSR signals with material from Suv39h dn ES cells as compared to wild-type ES cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of RNA from sucrose gradient fractions (Figure 5B).

claim: MSR RNA signals are higher in material from Suv39h double-null ES cells compared to wild-type ES cells in nucleosomal fractions.
source: This analysis identified progressive enrichment of MSR RNA in the nucleosome fractions but not in the nucleosome-free fractions and also revealed higher MSR signals with material from Suv39h dn ES cells as compared to wild-type ES cells (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR (Figure 5B).

claim: LINE L1MdA 5'UTR RNA does not show enrichment in nucleosome fractions versus nucleosome-free fractions.
source: This enrichment in the nucleosome fractions vs. nucleosome-free fractions was not observed for LINE L1MdA 5'UTR RNA.
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of sucrose gradient fractions (Figure 5B).

claim: Around 80% of total MSR RNA remain chromatin associated.
source: Subcellular isolation of RNA populations from cytoplasmic, nucleoplasmic and chromatin fractions further corroborated that around 80% of the total MSR RNA remain chromatin associated (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of subcellular fractions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).

claim: The relative ratio of chromatin-bound RNA versus nucleoplasmic RNA is highest for MSR RNA compared to other RNA repeat classes.
source: Although other RNA repeat classes, such as LINE L1MdA and SINE elements are also enriched in the chromatin fraction, the relative ratio of chromatin-bound RNA vs. nucleoplasmic RNA is highest for MSR RNA (Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of subcellular fractions (Figure 5—figure supplement 3B).

claim: MSR transcripts give rise to elevated reads in chromatin-derived (1800 mean counts) compared to nucleoplasmic (450 mean counts) cDNA libraries.
source: Although MSR reads are around 10–20 fold below the LINE L1MdA reads and significantly less than the more than 100 fold higher amount of SINE B1 reads, it is only the MSR transcripts that give rise to elevated reads in the chromatin-derived (1800 mean counts) as compared to the nucleoplasmic (450 mean counts) material (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by Hiseq RNA sequencing data (Figure 5C).

claim: LINE L1MdA and SINE B1 transcripts show similar mean counts in both chromatin-derived and nucleoplasmic cDNA libraries.
source: LINE L1MdA and SINE B1 transcripts show similar mean counts in both chromatin-derived and nucleoplasmic cDNA libraries, whereas minor satellite repeat RNA is the least abundant in chromatin but enriched in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Supported by Hiseq RNA sequencing data (Figure 5C).

claim: Minor satellite repeat RNA is the least abundant in chromatin but enriched in the nucleoplasm.
source: LINE L1MdA and SINE B1 transcripts show similar mean counts in both chromatin-derived and nucleoplasmic cDNA libraries, whereas minor satellite repeat RNA is the least abundant in chromatin but enriched in the nucleoplasm.
evidence: Supported by Hiseq RNA sequencing data (Figure 5C).

claim: Major satellite repeats are expressed from both strands.
source: Hiseq RNA sequencing data with nuclear RNA preparations from mouse ES cells further show that major satellite repeats are expressed from both strands (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and that the MSR display multiple transcriptional start sites (TSS) (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by strand-specific RNA-seq data (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).

claim: MSR display multiple transcriptional start sites (TSS).
source: Hiseq RNA sequencing data with nuclear RNA preparations from mouse ES cells further show that major satellite repeats are expressed from both strands (Figure 6—figure supplement 1) and that the MSR display multiple transcriptional start sites (TSS) (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by RNA-seq data and cited reference (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2012).

claim: MSR RNA is transcribed by RNA Polymerase II.
source: Additional analysis of MSR-repeat RNA indicated that it is transcribed by RNA Polymerase II, is not protected at the 5'end and largely lacks a poly(A) tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by RNA polymerase II inhibition experiments with α-amanitin and DRB (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).

claim: MSR RNA is not protected at the 5'end.
source: Additional analysis of MSR-repeat RNA indicated that it is transcribed by RNA Polymerase II, is not protected at the 5'end and largely lacks a poly(A) tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by terminator exonuclease treatment showing MSR RNA is degraded (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C).

claim: MSR RNA largely lacks a poly(A) tail.
source: Additional analysis of MSR-repeat RNA indicated that it is transcribed by RNA Polymerase II, is not protected at the 5'end and largely lacks a poly(A) tail (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by poly(A) selection experiments showing MSR RNA is not enriched in poly(A)+ fraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: Major satellite transcripts range from ~0.5 to >7 kb in size.
source: In agreement with previous observations (Lu and Gilbert, 2007), we detect a heterogeneous population of major satellite transcripts that range from ~0.5 to >7 kb (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot analysis (Figure 6A) and cited reference (Lu and Gilbert, 2007).

claim: Expression of major satellite RNA in the forward orientation is considerably higher than that for the reverse strand.
source: Expression of major satellite RNA in the forward orientation (detected by the AS probe) is considerably higher than that for the reverse strand and MSR transcripts are elevated in Suv39h dn ES cells.
evidence: Supported by Northern blot analysis with strand-specific probes (Figure 6A).

claim: MSR transcripts are elevated in Suv39h double-null ES cells.
source: Expression of major satellite RNA in the forward orientation (detected by the AS probe) is considerably higher than that for the reverse strand and MSR transcripts are elevated in Suv39h dn ES cells.
evidence: Supported by Northern blot analysis (Figure 6A).

claim: RNaseH treatment results in pronounced reduction of hybridization signal for both MSR strands.
source: We observe pronounced reduction of hybridization signal for both MSR strands upon RNaseH treatment and complete loss after RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot analysis of RNaseH-treated chromatin RNA (Figure 6A).

claim: RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion results in complete loss of MSR hybridization signal.
source: We observe pronounced reduction of hybridization signal for both MSR strands upon RNaseH treatment and complete loss after RNaseA (100 mM salt) digestion (Figure 6A, left panel).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot analysis (Figure 6A).

claim: LINE L1MdA RNA shows only minor reduction of hybridization signal upon RNaseH digestion.
source: LINE L1MdA RNA is also heterogeneous in size and transcribed from both strands. LINE L1MdA RNA is up-regulated in Suv39h dn ES cells, but RNaseH digestion only results in a minor reduction of the hybridization signal (Figure 6A, right panel).
evidence: Supported by Northern blot analysis (Figure 6A, right panel).

claim: RNaseH sensitivity is an intrinsic property of MSR RNA.
source: Further, extension of this analysis by using RT-qPCR with chromatin-associated RNA preparations reveals that the RNaseH sensitivity is an intrinsic property of MSR RNA, much less pronounced for LINE L1MdA RNA and not found for SINE B1 transcripts or single copy house-keeping genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR analysis of RNaseH-treated chromatin RNA (Figure 6B).

claim: RNaseH sensitivity is much less pronounced for LINE L1MdA RNA compared to MSR RNA.
source: Further, extension of this analysis by using RT-qPCR with chromatin-associated RNA preparations reveals that the RNaseH sensitivity is an intrinsic property of MSR RNA, much less pronounced for LINE L1MdA RNA and not found for SINE B1 transcripts or single copy house-keeping genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR (Figure 6B).

claim: RNaseH sensitivity is not found for SINE B1 transcripts or single copy house-keeping genes.
source: Further, extension of this analysis by using RT-qPCR with chromatin-associated RNA preparations reveals that the RNaseH sensitivity is an intrinsic property of MSR RNA, much less pronounced for LINE L1MdA RNA and not found for SINE B1 transcripts or single copy house-keeping genes (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by RT-qPCR (Figure 6B).

claim: MSR-RDIP signal is 2.1% in wild type ES cells and 3.2% in Suv39h double-null ES cells.
source: Quantification of MSR-RDIP signal indicated 2.1% (wild type ES cells) and 3.2% (Suv39h dn ES cells) of the input material to be enriched by the S9.6 antibody (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RDIP-qPCR analysis (Figure 6C).

claim: MSR-RDIP signal is drastically reduced by RNaseH treatment in both wild type and Suv39h double-null ES cells.
source: In RNaseH-treated samples, this signal was drastically reduced in both the wild type and Suv39h dn ES cell nucleic acid preparations.
evidence: Supported by RDIP-qPCR after RNaseH treatment (Figure 6C).

claim: LINE L1MdA 5'UTR sequences are enriched by the S9.6 antibody, particularly in Suv39h double-null ES cells.
source: LINE L1MdA 5'UTR sequences are also enriched, particularly in the Suv39h dn ES cell material, where they too are sensitive to RNaseH digestion.
evidence: Supported by RDIP-qPCR (Figure 6C).

claim: LINE L1MdA 5'UTR sequences enriched by S9.6 antibody are sensitive to RNaseH digestion.
source: LINE L1MdA 5'UTR sequences are also enriched, particularly in the Suv39h dn ES cell material, where they too are sensitive to RNaseH digestion.
evidence: Supported by RDIP-qPCR (Figure 6C).

claim: SINE B1 sequences do not appear to be reactive to the S9.6 antibody.
source: SINE B1 sequences do not appear to be reactive to the S9.6 antibody (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by RDIP-qPCR showing no enrichment (Figure 6C).

claim: Mouse heterochromatin contains large portions of non-coding major satellite repeat DNA elements.
source: Mouse heterochromatin contains large portions of non-coding major satellite repeat DNA elements (Hörz and Altenburger, 1981; Vissel and Choo, 1989).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Hörz and Altenburger, 1981; Vissel and Choo, 1989).

claim: Transcription from major satellite repeats is required to establish heterochromatin formation in the zygote and 2 to 4 cell embryonic stages.
source: In early mouse development, transcription from the major satellite repeats (MSR) is required to establish heterochromatin formation in the zygote and the 2 to 4 cell embryonic stages (Probst et al., 2010; Casanova et al., 2013; Burton and Torres-Padilla, 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Probst et al., 2010; Casanova et al., 2013; Burton and Torres-Padilla, 2014).

claim: Failure of MSR transcription results in abrogation of development of the early mouse embryo.
source: Failure of MSR transcription will not allow heterochromatin establishment and results in abrogation of the development of the early mouse embryo (Probst et al., 2010; Burton and Torres-Padilla, 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Probst et al., 2010; Burton and Torres-Padilla, 2014).

claim: In somatic mouse cells, heterochromatic transcription is cell cycle regulated and MSR transcripts transiently increase in late G1/early S phases.
source: In somatic mouse cells, heterochromatic transcription is cell cycle regulated and MSR transcripts transiently increase in the late G1/early S phases and persist during mitosis (Lu and Gilbert, 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Lu and Gilbert, 2007).

claim: MSR transcripts persist during mitosis.
source: In somatic mouse cells, heterochromatic transcription is cell cycle regulated and MSR transcripts transiently increase in the late G1/early S phases and persist during mitosis (Lu and Gilbert, 2007).
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Lu and Gilbert, 2007).

claim: RNaseA treatment of permeabilized mouse embryonic fibroblasts weakens heterochromatin and leads to dispersion of HP1.
source: Moreover, RNaseA treatment of permeabilized mouse embryonic fibroblasts (MEF) weakens heterochromatin and leads to dispersion of key heterochromatic factors, such as heterochromatin protein 1 (HP1) (Maison et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Maison et al., 2002).

claim: RNA binding has been shown for HP1.
source: For heterochromatin factors, RNA binding has been shown for HP1 (Muchardt et al., 2002; Maison et al., 2011), the Suv4-20h KMT (Bierhoff et al., 2014) and also for other heterochromatin-related proteins that are involved in X inactivation (Moindrot and Brockdorff, 2016) and Polycomb-mediated gene silencing (Bonasio et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Muchardt et al., 2002; Maison et al., 2011).

claim: RNA binding has been shown for the Suv4-20h KMT.
source: For heterochromatin factors, RNA binding has been shown for HP1 (Muchardt et al., 2002; Maison et al., 2011), the Suv4-20h KMT (Bierhoff et al., 2014) and also for other heterochromatin-related proteins that are involved in X inactivation (Moindrot and Brockdorff, 2016) and Polycomb-mediated gene silencing (Bonasio et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Bierhoff et al., 2014).

claim: The chromo domain of SUV39H1 binds to H3K9me3.
source: While the chromo domain of SUV39H1 has been shown to bind to H3K9me3 (Wang et al., 2012), the chromo domains of a number of proteins, for example MSL3 (Akhtar et al., 2000) and Chp1 (Ishida et al., 2012) can also bind RNA in addition to their interaction with modified histones.
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Wang et al., 2012).

claim: The chromo domains of MSL3 and Chp1 can bind RNA in addition to their interaction with modified histones.
source: While the chromo domain of SUV39H1 has been shown to bind to H3K9me3 (Wang et al., 2012), the chromo domains of a number of proteins, for example MSL3 (Akhtar et al., 2000) and Chp1 (Ishida et al., 2012) can also bind RNA in addition to their interaction with modified histones.
evidence: Supported by cited references (Akhtar et al., 2000; Ishida et al., 2012).

claim: De novo silencing of intact LINE elements may require the synergistic activity of both Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 enzymes.
source: It should be noted, however, that silencing of another prominent Suv39h target, long intergenic nuclear elements (LINE) (Bulut-Karslioglu et al., 2014), was not restored by any of the Suv39h-EGFP products (Figure 2—figure supplement 1). Thus, in contrast to MSR, de novo silencing of intact LINE elements may require the synergistic activity of both Suv39h1 and Suv39h2 enzymes.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that individual Suv39h enzymes cannot restore LINE silencing (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claim: An RNA-nucleosome scaffold is the physiological template for the stable association of Suv39h enzymes to chromatin.
source: These data reveal an RNA component to be important for the recruitment of the Suv39h KMT and suggest that an RNA-nucleosome scaffold is the physiological template for the stable association of Suv39h enzymes to chromatin.
evidence: Inferred from the RNA-dependent association of Suv39h enzymes with poly-nucleosomes (Figure 5A) and the loss of this association upon RNase treatment.

claim: Mouse heterochromatin is composed of a higher order RNA-nucleosome scaffold that contains MSR RNA:DNA hybrids and significant portions of single-stranded MSR-repeat RNA.
source: We propose a model, in which mouse heterochromatin is composed of a higher order RNA-nucleosome scaffold that contains MSR RNA:DNA hybrids and significant portions of single-stranded MSR-repeat RNA.
evidence: Based on integration of multiple experimental findings: MSR RNA chromatin association, RNaseH sensitivity, SHAPE analysis showing ssRNA regions, and RDIP detection of RNA:DNA hybrids.
